Initially designed as part of a telerehabilitation system, Flo enables remote interaction between clinicians and patients while facilitating demonstration of rehabilitation activities [23]. Previous studies found Flo effective in comparison to traditional telepresence method [24] and has potential use for exploring MNS activation during AO tasks [11]. This proof-of-concept paper presents the latest advancements in Flo robot (Flo version 2), aimed at improving its suitability for AO therapy, and a case study to assess the use of upgraded system in AO paradigms and investigate the neurophysiological effects of observing various robot actions using EEG.

Factors such as the human-like appearance of the agent and types of actions in visual stimuli during AO affect neural responses in the MNS [7]. Several studies used different types of robots, such as robotic arms [8], [9] and humanoid robots [10], [11] in AO paradigms and analyzed the MNS responses to actions performed by robots versus by humans [12]. The MNS shows varying responses to human and robot actions, with generally stronger activation for human agents in simple movements [8], [13], [14]. However, complex and goal-oriented actions elicit similar MNS responses to both agents, particularly in the parietal and premotor regions [15], [16], [17], [10]. These ﬁndings suggest that the potential use of robots for neurorehabilitation such as AO therapy. Regarding the concept of transitivity during AO, transitive actions involve interaction with objects in the peripersonal space (e.g., grasping a ball), while intransitive actions are simple hand-arm movements that do not involve objects (e.g., waving). Human MNS typically displays greater responses in frontal and parietal MNS and motor cortex to transitive than intransitive actions [18], [19]. EEG studies indicate that MNS responses to transitive actions of the human hand induce greater mu suppression in the C3 channel compared to intransitive actions [20].

secao: III. EVALUATING FLO V2 IN AO THERAPY > A. Experimental Design and Protocol
trecho: This case study recruited three right-handed participants, ages 23 to 24, with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders, to explore the neurophysiological effects of observing various robot-performed actions on the mirror neuron system (MNS). This study was approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board (IRB No. 830126) on June 29, 2021. Participants completed two experiments in order: a videobased and an in-person robot action observation and execution (AOE) experiment. In the video-based experiment (Fig. 6(a)), pre-recorded videos of actions performed by the Flo v2 robot were presented as visual stimuli using the opensource software PsychoPy[29]. In the in-person experiment (Fig. 6(b)), the Flo v2 robot performed actions directly, with the LED matrix on its chest indicating task stages, and the system was administered by the aforementioned AOE program. For both experiments, participants observed 10second arm actions of different types (i.e., seven unimanual actions for each arm and four bimanual actions, see Table II) consisting of a 1000 ms stationary pre-action, an 8000 ms action observation interval, and a 1000 ms stationary postaction. Each stimulus was repeated four times and presented in a counterbalanced block design (Fig. 6c), each block contained a sequence of trials. Each trial began with a 1000 ms ﬁxation cross, followed by the stimulus, another 1000 ms ﬁxation cross, and a 5000 ms action execution interval indicated by a triangle shape. The video-based experiment included six blocks of 12 trials each. In the in-person experiment, the ﬁrst six blocks featured the 12 intransitive actions including four unimanual actions for each arm and four bimanual actions, and the ﬁnal six blocks each featured one of the six transitive actions (i.e, two for each arm).

Integration of a Gripper-Equipped Humanoid Social Robot for EEG-Monitored Action Observation Paradigms Anh T. Nguyen, Member, IEEE1, Hao Zhang2, Tian Tan2, Mohammad Abrar1, Yuxin Zhang3, and Michelle J. Johnson, Member, IEEE4 Abstract— Action Observation (AO) therapy leverages the mirror neuron system (MNS) and may support motor recovery in neurorehabilitation. In this study, we integrated Flo v2, a humanoid robot equipped with grippers and object detection system, into an AO therapy paradigm with electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring. Flo v2’s enhanced design enables the execution of upper-limb actions, either transitive (involving object interaction such as grasping a cup) or intransitive (gesturebased without object manipulation such as waving). The robot control is synchronized with EEG recording to facilitate the investigation of cortical responses during AO tasks. We also conducted a case study to assess of the upgraded robot system’s feasibility. Three healthy participants observed and imitated robot-performed actions, where the robot actor was in person or on videos. Exploratory analyses of EEG signals examined sensorimotor mu event-related desynchronization (ERD) during video-based and in-person AO tasks. Results indicated stronger responses during bimanual and transitive AO in the in-person settings. However, individual variability in cortical responses was evident, with one subject showing less pronounced ERD patterns, and that comparisons of mu ERDs across different types of action in video-based AO settings were inconsistent among subjects. Flo v2’s enhancements demonstrated its feasibility as a tool for robot-mediated AOE therapy and highlighted potential for further neurorehabilitation research.

The tool used in this study is the companion robot-assisted app for children with asthma, named “Pukkabot,” an innovative device designed to teach proper inhaler use and promote medication adherence through positive reinforcement (Figure 1). The design of the companion robot is tailored to each child’s treatment plan, specifically focusing on those who require both inhaled controller medications and quick-relief medications. The app operates on the Android 13 platform, featuring a touch-sensitive screen that displays both video and audio content. The model, shaped like an animal, measures 23.5 cm in width, 23.1 cm in length, 21 cm in height, and 800 g in weight, including the screen. Its structure is composed of polylactic acid plastic, providing strength and lightweight durability during use. Polylactic acid is a form of plastic derived from natural sources, making it non-irritating during use. It can be cleaned with an alcohol spray. The model is developed to be placed on a flat surface, with the weight supported by its 2 legs and tail for balance while using the screen. The screen area is recessed by approximately 2 inches to prevent damage in case of impact or if it falls from a height. The main display screen provides the following 5 operational modes. The researcher instructed the caregiver and the child to interact with the companion robot. The process began with the caregiver setting a medication reminder (set for 5 min) and selecting an air quality monitoring option within the app, which displays the real-time Air Quality Index (AQI) to raise awareness about environmental triggers. Afterward, the child was invited to select a preferred pet (rabbit, dog, cat, bear, and dragon). When the reminder alarm was triggered, the child practiced medication administration steps by following on-screen instructions, using an empty inhaler device that contained no active medication. This activity was conducted solely as a demonstration to simulate proper inhaler technique, without actual medication use. The demonstration lasted approximately 5 minutes, during which the researcher provided verbal guidance and support. The entire process was completed within approximately 15 minutes. Afterward, the caregivers were instructed to complete a 10-item System Usability Scale (SUS) regarding the companion robot. The caregivers completed the questionnaire, whereas the researcher recorded personal information from the patient’s medical records. Finally, the researcher interviewed the caregivers to gather their attitudes toward using the asthma management companion robot, as well as any perceived barriers or facilitators to its implementation. This aimed to determine areas for system improvement. The interview included 6 questions and lasted approximately 5‐10 minutes.

secao: Methods > Research Instruments > System Usability Scale (SUS)
trecho: The SUS, developed by John Brooke in 1986 [17], is a widely recognized tool for evaluating the usability and overall satisfaction of a companion robot-assisted app. The SUS consists of a 5-point Likert scale, with response options ranging from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 5 (“strongly agree”). The scale includes 10 items—5 positively worded and 5 negatively worded—that assess the usability of the asthma management app. Scoring involves assigning values from 1 to 5 for the positive items while applying reverse scoring for negative items. The total score is calculated and then multiplied by 2.5 to convert the range from 0 to 40 to a scale of 0‐100. A score of ≥68 indicates acceptable usability, corresponding to the 50th percentile, whereas scores below this threshold indicate areas for improvement in design and usability [17-19].

Quang, Yun, and Choi have achieved smooth interactions between multiple people and a robot by making a complex use of multiple microphones and Kinectcompatible infrared sensors [2]. Cech, Mittal and Deleforge improved the human recognition accuracy by combining robot-camera captured images and sound source localization with multiple microphones [3]. The abovementioned robots used sound source localization; however, they did not actively react to humans on their own. On the other hand, there are a number of studies available on the methods of interaction with robots imitating animals. Koay et al. were inspired by dog reactions to establish a scenario for a robot that “performs to human reactions” to materialize natural human-robot interactions [4]. Speciﬁcally, a robot, consisting of a head installed with a camera and a body ﬁtted with wheels, ﬁrst turned its head toward a subject, and then decided its own actions based upon the subject actions. Singh and Young developed a robot installed with a mechanism that imitates an animal tail to achieve smooth interactions with humans [5]. Yohanan and MacLean have attempted interactions by manually touching a furry robot to give it a stimulus of human sensitivity [6]. Moyle et al. have studied how effective animal-like robots would be on senile people with dementia [7]. None of the above-mentioned studies, however, have used sound source localization techniques. During the design of a robotic pet, we considered the furry surface of the robots used by Yohanan et al. and Moyle et al. A robot without fur, as in the work of Cech et al. [3] could have an improved human recognition accuracy through a combined processing of microphone and camera data. However, a robot with fur could cause its camera visual ﬁeld to be obstructed by the fur piles. In the interactions between humans and robotic pets, robots are expected to respond with regard to human actions or to surrounding circumstances. Although humans can recognize robots or the environment using various senses, such as the visual sense, the auditory sense, and the tactile sense, and can express themselves vocally and verbally, robots have technical and economic constraints in their perception or their means of expression. None of the past successful cases of human-robotic pet interaction has ever tried to generate communications from nothing but sound source localizations with a robot audition system and its own movements. Considering the above, we developed a robotic pet by combining a simple moving mechanism and the robot audition system HARK (Honda Research Institute Japan Audition for Robots with Kyoto University) [1], which separates and localizes sound sources using the input from the microphone array. Given that the developed robotic pet does not express its feelings by wagging its tail, uttering voices or by ex- pressing itself in different forms, we observed how it could manage to interact and communicate with humans, relying only on its high-performance audition system and its minimal moving mechanism.

Although humans can recognize robots or the environment using various senses, such as the visual sense, the auditory sense, and the tactile sense, and can express themselves vocally and verbally, robots have technical and economic constraints in their perception or their means of expression. trecho: The first robot selected for the study, iRobiQ, is a small sized humanoid robot produced by Yujin Robotics equipped with a tablet computer that can play video and animation in the front panel (Fig. 2(a)). It is used both as an educational robot and as a service robot (Shin et al., 2008). iRobiQ can generate behaviors such as singing, talking and dancing required for communication with children. It can move its head, arms, and wheels, but does not change its position in our experiments despite of having this ability. It is 45-cm tall, and has a camera and sound devices such as a speaker and a microphone, and a touch sensor on its Liquid Crystal Display (LCD) chest panel. It has 3 Degrees of Freedom (DOFs) on its head and 1 DOF on each arm. The robot has facial light-emitting diodes (LEDs) as part of its own hardware system and can display five types of facial expressions: shy, disappointed, neutral, happy, and surprised. To realize natural communication with a robot, traditional human communication has to be imitated by providing by gestures, speaking, touch, etc. To improve the expression ability of the robot, we associated body gestures with facial expressions. We enabled the robot to execute the same sequence of commands during the treatment of each child. All multimedia contents are implemented in Adobe Flash to display on the LCD screen of the robot. Basic robot behaviors are programmed using ROCOS Studio, which is a platform to author robot contents, and the transactions that allow the operator to manage these contents are prepared.

secao: 3. Methods > 3.3. Design of the robotic system
trecho: We evaluate the proposed design by using two robots with different appearance and capabilities. iRobiQ is a toy-like robot equipped with a digital display for animations, able to show facial expressions and gestures, allowing for visually rich communication. In contrast, Nao has a more humanoid appearance without a display and conveys empathy primarily through body posture, head movement, and speech intonation. A detailed comparison of the two robots is provided in Table 2. The objective is to compare different robot interfaces, and the results will also provide contribution in the HRI field. We expect the robots to show differences in their ability of drawing children’s attention. We enable the robot to perform simple body movements such as nodding, waving, dancing, and facial expressions. Because the robot will be placed in a fixed position in the clinic (Fig. 1), without posing any danger to humans; changing the robot’s position is intentionally not programmed, although it is possible by the robot’s wheels/legs. Before proceeding to real tests, a set of age-appropriate animations and educational videos were selected for iRobiQ to display on its chest screen. Animations used during dental procedures consisted of items that were popular among children and the videos focused on oral hygiene topics such as tooth brushing and the importance of dental care, and have been previously used in pediatric dentistry. The videos consisted of colorful cartoon-style animations with animal and child characters, using cheerful music and simple, playful storylines to engage children. Selection was guided by input from pediatric dental specialists to ensure that the material aligned with the cognitive and emotional levels of the target age group (6–10 years old). All children Fig. 1. secao: 3. Methods > 3.3. Design of the robotic system
trecho: An objective of the study is to equip a robot with natural language perception and understanding abilities so that it can comfort anxious children by conducting a conversation. Human acceptance of a companion robot is an important issue for long-term interaction, the robot must be able to communicate with people in a natural and human-like way and be excellent in performing its tasks (Leite et al., 2013). Given the constraints of dental procedures where children are often unable to speak freely, verbal interaction during treatment was typically limited to brief responses from the child. While the current WoZ system allows the operator to recognize alternative, non-verbal communication strategies, such as facial expressions, grunts, gestures or nods, fully autonomous systems would require real-time multimodal perception capabilities, enabling more responsive and context-aware interaction during treatment. Our proposed method relies on both verbal and non-verbal interaction between the children and the robot, and flexibility to make the children involved in the interaction by combining visual and auditory stimuli. Some children briefly touched the robot (e.g., its hand or head) during the initial introduction phase, if they wished, but tactile interaction was not a structured component of the study. The use of multi-sensory strategies has been shown to provide a significantly positive impact on anxiety compared to the use of a single stimulus (Khandelwal et al., 2019; Nuvvula et al., 2015).

Once the setup of the system was completed, the experimenters did not need to make any adjustments, such as reactivating the robot for each phase. The robots were operated to perform relevant body movements with facial expressions and played a role as a member of both the welcoming and the treatment team. In this scope, a sample communication scenario between a robot and a child is given in Appendix B. In the third phase, post-treatment, the robot thanked the child, encouraged her/him to visit again, and waved goodbye at the end of the treatment.

In robot groups, we placed the robots on a platform at the child’s eye level. The treatment procedure is visualized in Fig. 4 showing each phase step by step. Different distraction tools were applied in each phase. For example, when the child was exposed to treatment, there is no need to make eye contact with the child, and the robot explains the procedure, such as what the dentist was doing and why, in a fun way. During the time periods that the dentist takes a short break after applying filling or cleaning the tooth decay, the robot performs body and facial expressions, plays videos (only iRobiQ) or sings while dancing to distract the child’s mind. The participants were introduced to the robots in the pre-treatment phase, and familiarized themselves with the dental clinic equipment. In the during-treatment phase, the robots chatted with the child, instructed the child before and during the treatment, distracted and encouraged her/him, and only iRobiQ also played short animated videos, which included colorful cartoon characters, cheerful music, and narration. These animations were selected from pediatric dentistry materials and aimed to entertain while delivering messages about oral hygiene and reducing dental anxiety. Taking into account the multiple interactive factors that may influence the human–robot interaction, all of the participants spent the same amount of time interacting with a robot in the same way and the wizard was always the same person to have no effect on the attitude and behaviors of clinicians in using the robots. We programmed iRobiQ robot in order to execute the motion commands as distraction strategies (shaking head, swinging arms, face expressions) during the treatment. Nao robot expressed emotions through dynamic body movements and speech intonation rather than facial expressions. We created some animations and behaviors to enable robots to move and react interactively. Figs. 5(c) and 5(d) show some body movements performed by the Nao and iRobiQ robots, respectively.

In addition to measuring the children’s anxiety and behavior, in the robot groups, we have asked the children the question ‘‘Would you like to have the robot in your next treatment session?’’. Responses were given on a 5-point scale from ‘‘not at all’’(1) to ‘‘very much’’(5) (Beran et al., 2013). Changes in pulse rates between treatment phases, in addition to other measures, namely FIS, FBRS, and robot demand, collectively contribute to evaluating the overall human–robot interaction in terms of efficiency, effectiveness, and user satisfaction during dental treatment.

This study attempts to answer this research question: ‘‘Can a socially assistive robot help children cope with anxiety during their dental treatment better than conventional intervention methods?’’. The significance of using socially assistive robots as a new behavior management (distraction) method is investigated. Our main hypotheses for this experimental study are as follows. H1: Interacting with a companion robot during a dental procedure will reduce children’s anxiety and enhance their cooperation compared to conventional behavior management methods. H2: Different robot interaction modalities will lead to varying levels of anxiety reduction, reflecting the influence of design features on children’s responses during dental treatment. The evaluation criteria of the child robot interaction are focused on the classic Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) usability evaluation factors (ISO 9241-11), that are: efficiency, effectiveness, and user satisfaction. We evaluate the proposed robot interaction in terms of these three factors as listed in Table 1, and detailed in Section 4.2. Physiological heart rate can be an indicator of the efficiency of the child-robot interaction. It has been found that there is a relationship between dental anxiety and heart rate (Fernandez-Aguilar et al., 2020). Facial Image Scale measures the child’s emotional response, providing insights into the effectiveness of the robot in eliciting positive emotions or reducing negative ones. A positive facial image scale would indicate the effectiveness of the robot in creating a positive emotional impact. Frankl’s Behavior Rating Scale assesses the child’s cooperative behavior during the treatment. Effectiveness can be inferred from the scale by observing positive behavioral changes, indicating the success of the robot interaction. The questionnaire regarding the future demand for robots in dental visits assesses user satisfaction by measuring the child’s interest, comfort, and preference for having the robot around during dental treatments. Positive responses demonstrate user satisfaction and acceptance.

secao: 2. Related work > 2.3. Wizard of Oz experiments in human-robot interaction
trecho: The scope of social robots in health and education appears to be comprehensive, but there are still limitations. The development of autonomous robots often takes significant time and effort. Although autonomy is often considered the ultimate aim of robots, focusing only on autonomy may prevent exploration of the space of interaction design. In the field of human–robot interaction (HRI), many researchers use Wizard of Oz as an experimental technique to conduct robot interaction studies (Mai et al., 2011; Sirithunge et al., 2018; Strazdas et al., 2020; Schulz et al., 2022). For example, Huggable is a robotic companion developed to be used for applications in healthcare, education, and social communication, and helps mitigate stress, anxiety, and pain (Stiehl et al., 2009). It is capable of expressing verbal and non-verbal behaviors through Wizard of Oz teleoperation from a remote laptop computer. A humanoid robot of child size, KASPAR has been designed to be used as a social mediator, encouraging and helping children with autism interact and communicate with adults and other children. It has the ability to participate in a variety of interactive play scenarios, such as turn-taking or imitation (Boccanfuso et al., 2017). A telepresence robot, Mebot has social expressions, allows more enjoyable interaction, and communicates not only using just audio or video, but also utilizes expressive gestures, body pose, and proxemics (Adalgeirsson and Breazeal, 2010).

Robots must be well designed to work within the environment they are intended. The importance in this case is in designers working with social scientists, health professionals, and people for which the robot is intended, so that the approach is user-centered to ensure the robot meets a need, is reliable in accomplishing the tasks to meet the need, is concerned with the limitations of the audience for which it is intended, is an appropriate size and shape that can fit within the intended environment, and is made of materials and colors that look appealing. The look and appeal of robots is an area that often is ignored by developers and yet our work constantly convinces us that older adults in particular want a robot that looks friendly, offers tactile comfort (even if this is not the main purpose of the robot), and has features such as buttons and screens that can easily be manipulated with arthritic hands, impaired vision and cognitive decline.

Design features can impede the use of robots in the nursing home environment. Our team has been testing a number of robots. The team suggests there are features robotic designers need to consider when developing robots for use for older people and in particular people with dementia. Designers must understand the perceptual, motor control and cognitive capabilities of users and, in this case, their carers who are the people often responsible for assisting with using the robot. The robots we have been testing arrive either with sophisticated manuals explaining in detail the robot set up; limited instruction manuals; or manuals translated from a foreign language into English. In every case these need re-writing. The manuals can sometimes prove to be too sophisticated for the average user. The ageing process, staff and carers with limited education, and the dementing process may also result in the need for lay instructional manuals that enable users to effectively interact with the social robots. Prior to testing the robots, time is often spent by the research team in writing new instructional manuals alongside our research protocols, using photographs, diagrams and process steps that are tested prior to commencing the research. To assist with access and use there have also been times the researchers have attached cue cards to the robot to remind the user of the steps to follow.

A. Thomas and PARO Thomas is 82 years old. He has moderate to late stage dementia and he has lived in a nursing home north of Brisbane, Australia since his daughter Susan found she could no longer meet his care needs. The care staff describes Thomas as a pleasant man who is no bother as, following his hygiene needs each morning; he sits in a lounge chair and waits patiently to be taken back to his room in the evening. He interacts and talks to no one and he has limited facial expression. The care staff believes there is little that they need to do for Thomas, as he seems content. His daughter, however, believes the care staff has limited time to spend with Thomas and he lacks stimulation and this has resulted in his current state of apathy. Susan volunteers Thomas to become involved in research involving a therapeutic emotional response robot – PARO. Artificial intelligence software changes the robot’s behaviors based on an array of sensors that monitor sound, light, temperature and touch. It responds to sounds, can learn its name and learns to respond to words its owner uses frequently. It can show emotions such as surprise, happiness and anger and will cry if it is not receiving sufficient attention. It produces sounds similar to a real baby seal and is active during the day and asleep at night.

This paper explores the challenges of testing the efficacy of social robots in the nursing home environment. The findings of two projects exploring the use of PARO and Giraff (a telepresence robot) are outlined. The challenges experienced by the researchers when undertaking a randomized controlled trial and using a case study design to test the social robots with people with dementia are examined. While randomized controlled trials are advocated, in early testing of the social robots the case study approach has the advantage that researchers can manipulate and adjust the intervention as issues arise. This can assist in the preparation of a protocol for testing in a randomized controlled trial at a later date.

trecho: The researchers have been testing several animal and telepresence robots to determine their efficacy and feasibility for use with people with dementia living in nursing home settings. The most popular research design being used by the team to test efficacy are randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and in initial piloting for feasibility, a case study approach. The remainder of this paper will outline the challenges of testing the efficacy and feasibility of two social robots; PARO and Giraff.

The companion robot used in this study was a 28-cm, pumpkinsuited humanoid robot called Kabochan (Figure 1). Its appearance, voice, and motions resemble a 3-year-old boy. Kabochan is equipped with sensors in its mouth, head, hands, feet, and body, which allow it to interact via talking, singing, and head nodding in response to different stimulations (eg, striking, shaking, and spoken words).15 We hypothesized that participants in the Kabochan intervention group would demonstrate greater improvement during trial phases in 3 primary outcomes (neuropsychiatric symptoms and its associated caregiving distress, and depressive symptoms) and 3 secondary outcomes (cognitive ability, functional dependency, and quality of life) than participants in the usual-care control group would. Second, as the current intervention was nonfacilitated, residents had different levels of engagement frequency and duration with the robot. This variation in “intervention dosage” could have inﬂuenced our results. Future studies must also explore the dosage effect and determine the optimal intervention dosage. Third, Kabochan is a Japanese-speaking robot, and its effect and engagement would be impaired when used in a Chinese-speaking culture. A future study might examine its effects in different cultures and/or investigate whether the robot’s language has any impact on outcomes.

Some participants in this study refused to interact with Kabochan, whereas others developed a strong social attachment to it. Giving and withdrawing Kabochan may evoke strong negative verbal and behavioral responses. secao: RESULTS > Perceptions of health care professionals
trecho: Desired technological characteristics. General characteristics: HCPs had differing opinions about the technology’s appearance. Some said a human form would be ideal to support users in executing movements and that it should have precise joints in order to demonstrate specific movements correctly. Some argued that a desktop design [33] or a system with a screen and camera would be enough to supervise exercise performance and be less intimidating than a human form robot. It would be useful to provide visual feedback about users’ exertion and visually demonstrate exercises. HCPs mentioned that the technology should be easy to move around inside and outside the home and easy to store. They added that it should be easy to understand and use, otherwise it would be hard for people with severe impairments to use it. Customized to user’s preferences and needs: HCPs said the technology’s voice and exercise suggestions should vary according to the user’s preferences and needs. They mentioned that the technology’s voice should be adapted to users’ emotions and that exercise options should match users’ capacities. Technological characteristics: HCPs mentioned that the technology should be frequently updated and should incorporate medical knowledge about the users’ condition in order to appropriately supervise their exercise performance and suggest exercises corresponding to their fluctuating capacities. They also maintained that the technology should visually support users during exertion (e.g., with a screen) or allow telerehabilitation. Finally, HCPs said the technology should allow them to consult the clients’ exercise profile so they could modify the exercise program through an information transfer (e.g., removable memory card) or graphic report.

Desired technological characteristics. General characteristics: Clients commented on the system’s physical appearance. A majority preferred a human form because of its realism although they liked the desktop design [33] shown in the video; it was considered original and attractive. One client argued that it would be ideal to incorporate the technology with the exercise equipment (C1). Clients had differing opinions about the size of the technology but generally they wanted an appropriate size and weight to be able to move it and store it easily at home. To ensure a long operating life, they said the technology should be robust and reliable. Price is a crucial issue: it must be affordable. Finally, they maintained that the technology must be easy to use and understand, which would be enhanced by using vocal interaction with the system rather than touch commands. Customized to user’s preferences and needs: Clients said that customization of the technology is important with respect to voice type and exercise options. They argued that users should have the option to select the system’s voice from a range of choices and that the system’s voice tone should be adapted to the user’s mood. One client pointed out that the technology’s language must be adapted to that of the user to make the interaction more personal (C5). Finally, it was mentioned that the technology should be flexible in managing exercises to increase users’ intention to use the technology: several exercise options (varying types and levels of difficulty) should be offered to match the user’s mood, energy level and capacities.

A key to the success of socially assistive robots is their multiple interaction modes with the user, such as dialog, visual recognition, type of voice, and body movement. One gap that has been identified is the need to improve the technology’s social skills [25], namely its ability to recognize speech and detect emotions so as to achieve more natural human-machine interactions. Refining these two elements could help to personalize the interaction even more, process audio information more quickly and improve the dialog flow. However, it is not known how a socially assistive robot with speech recognition and emotion detection capabilities could be used to improve adherence to home-based rehabilitation exercises. Thus, there is a need to explore how natural human-robot interaction could help individuals with chronic neurological conditions. With a view to potentially benefiting from these new capabilities, the first objective of this study was to explore how a robot that offers supervision and encouragement could increase adherence to home-based long-term rehabilitation exercises for individuals with neurological conditions. The second objective was to identify perceived obstacles and facilitators related to using a robot with artificial audition capabilities. These results will be used to guide the design and optimization of robot audition technology. A qualitative research design was used. Focus groups were conducted with two categories of informants: (1) individuals with a stable chronic neurological condition, and (2) health care professionals. Focus groups are particularly relevant to collect points of view about a new technology and facilitate conversations between participants [26]. This approach can be used to explore whether participants see potential uses, how they understand the product, if they like it or not, and what the potential barriers to its use are [27].

Thematic content analysis was used to capture the meaning of the discussions. Focus group transcripts were reviewed for accuracy against the recordings. QDA Miner software was used to perform the content analysis. Main concepts from the data were determined, preliminary categories were compared and grouped under broader categories and subcategories. Then the findings were linked with the theoretical models. To ensure trustworthiness, the second author and a student researcher independently identified themes, which were then validated by team consensus through a coding review with the principal investigator.

First, as in all qualitative research, we cannot generalize our results since the sampling method was purposive rather than random. Second, it was challenging to find the right balance between showing concrete scenarios demonstrating the technology’s capacities and letting participants imagine their own solutions. Although we supervised the discussion with an ideal creative frame of mind, it is unclear to what extent the realism of the images shown influenced the participants’ perceptions regarding the technology and if it accurately evoked the technology’s potential. In fact, we felt some images caused some discomfort among some of the participants, especially HCPs (e.g., they laughed a lot and identified several barriers to its use compared to clients). Third, the clients recruited were already performing exercises and were looking for solutions to increase their adherence. It is possible that this influenced their motivation to participate in the study.

Through the personalisation of the robot, we aimed to increase the perceived sociability and social presence of the robot, and increase the patient’s motivation, engagement and adherence. The video analysis shows that the gaze and social interaction with the robot were maintained throughout the CR programme, which is a valuable result showing that the patient did not lose interest in the robot throughout the long-term rehabilitation. Moreover, the patient (as well as the medical staff) acknowledged the robot as a social agent instead of just a tool, by verbally and non-verbally interacting with it. A detailed analysis of the perceived personalised aspects of the system showed that the patient positively reacted to the positive progress motivation given at the end of the session for having a lower number of problems in the session with “Let’s keep up the good work!”. In fact, the patient verbally thanked the robot in three of these cases, which did not happen towards the other non-personalised behaviours. The patient negatively reacted to the misidentiﬁcations in user recognition, which may further support the social agent perspective, however, he very positively responded to the corresponding UTAUT question as well as to the other personalisation aspects, which suggests that personalisation mitigates the negative user experience [29]. While the positive formulation of the Bond category of WAI also shows that the sociability of the robot was perceived highly positive throughout the CR programme, the negative formulation shows an increase in the social presence of the robot, based on the detailed analysis that indicated the fear of losing cooperation, and hence increased pressure to comply with the robot. In addition, even though the patient was mostly focused throughout the training stage, thereby limiting the gaze, the numbers indicate that the patient paid attention to the robot, thereby recognising its presence.

secao: IV. CASE STUDY > C. Long-term Perception of the Robot
trecho: Qualitative data was collected using the WAI questionnaire at the middle and end of the study, in order to analyse the long-term perception of the robot by the patient (Fig. 6). Results showed that the perception for Goal, Task and Bond was maintained highly positive throughout the CR programme, supporting our objectives with personalisation of the robot. Working Alliance Inventory (WAI) responses evaluated at the middle of the CR programme (18th session) and the ﬁnal (35th) session. In the case of negative formulation, the results decrease in Task and Goal category. These outcomes show that the negative perception of the robot decreases with time. The patient is less confused with the tasks (corrections) made by the robot during the rehabilitation, and the patient believes that the time spent with the robot is proﬁtable more over 4Conforming to normative behaviours to gain approval of another person. the duration of the CR programme. Regarding the Bond, the negative perception worsen slightly. Detailed analysis of the open questions showed that the patient felt that the robot would no longer cooperate with him during the sessions if he did not make the corrections requested by the robot (e.g., cervical posture and the high HR conﬁrmation). The UTAUT questionnaire [13] results support that the patient perceived the robot and the CR programme as highly positive, strongly agreeing with 88.5% of the questions and agreeing with the social presence aspects and the robot’s utility in therapy development, which is more positive than the perceptions of the non-personalised robot in [13]. Additionally, the personalisation aspects were all very positively perceived and enjoyed. The responses to the open questions further support the ﬁndings: “I would recommend using the robot as it is a great help during the CR programme”, “The robot interacts in a positive way with me, it helps me along with the medical staff, and it is also a good tool for them”.

Regarding the number of warnings for cervical posture correction (in Fig. 4), the video analysis showed that the patient corrected his posture without fail upon a simple prompt by the robot. While the gaze and social interaction were higher at the initial sessions due to possibly the novelty effect and the adjustment process to the technology, these interactions also occurred throughout the later sessions. Additionally, the video analysis showed that the patient is very focused on the exercise as expected, hence, the patient could mostly only look at the robot at the beginning of the treadmill exercise and at the end of the cooldown stage, which could have resulted in the low number of gaze and social interactions depending on the session intensity. Various types of social interaction were observed, such as talking to the robot (at session 33), mirroring the robot’s gesture to the Call medical staff alert, reacting positively (e.g., smiling or thanking the robot) to the motivational feedback of the robot, touching (caressing) the robot (e.g., at the end of a session after the robot “sighed” going into sleep mode), talking to other patients about the robot’s role and its beneﬁts, and reacting negatively (e.g., frown) to the robot, in the case of misidentiﬁcations from user recognition, posture correction (once) and for the high number of alerts to the medical staff. The user recognition performed poorly (14 out of 38 times5), due to the malfunctioning face recognition (13 times), including the ﬁrst (enrolment) session of the patient. Since the user recognition uses online learning, this negatively affected the performance of the system. Nonetheless, the video analysis shows that out of 9 misidentiﬁcations, the patient reacted negatively only twice (i.e., the other times, he did not react). Moreover, the patient strongly agreed with The robot recognises me correctly in UTAUT.

Interaction results of the video analysis based on 30 sessions2. We analysed 30 recorded sessions2 to observe the interactions with the robot throughout the CR programme (Fig. 7). Four types of interactions were analysed by an independent coder: (i) Medical staff interaction with the robot, which occurs when the medical staff interact with the robot either through responding to the robot’s request for intervention during a critical high HR, or talks with the robot when checking the patient, (ii) Posture correction upon robot request, (iii) Gaze which indicates when the patient looks at the robot to pay attention and (iv) Social interaction that consists of the patient’s verbal (e.g., thanking the robot after the personalised progress feedback given at the end of the session) and non-verbal (e.g., gesture to the robot after motivational feedback, or touch the head of the robot) communications with the robot. The medical staff worked collaboratively with the robot to intervene in the sessions when necessary, such as for the 13th session which is discernible in Fig. 7, or to change the exercise intensity. secao: III. METHODOLOGY > A. Socially Assistive Robot in Cardiac Rehabilitation
trecho: We designed and integrated a fully autonomous socially assistive robot with this sensor interface to enable giving verbal feedback and motivation [9]. We used a NAO2 robot (SoftBank Robotics Europe) as shown in Fig. 1. The various types of robot’s feedback and requests are as follows: (i) announcing the session parameters (speed and inclination of the treadmill) at the beginning of a session, (ii) motivating the patient throughout the session (e.g., “Let’s go! You can do it!”), (iii) requesting for entry of the Borg scale on the tablet interface at certain periods, (iv) tracking and warning high HR and requesting conﬁrmation from the patient of his health status, (v) requesting correction of the cervical posture to reduce risk of dizziness and falls, (vi) alerting the medical staff in case of exceeded HR or BS values. The warning and critical alert thresholds of HR and BS are determined by the physiatrists based on the progress of the patient throughout the CR sessions. While the high HR warning does not represent a critical situation, it can give an initial warning to the medical staff about the patient’s condition. When the medical staff intervenes for the critical HR or BS alert, he/she should touch the head of the robot to end the alert. The Borg requests and high HR conﬁrmation are compulsory, i.e., the robot repeatedly requests these parameters if the patient does not respond within a given time.

Through the personalisation of the robot, we aimed to increase the perceived sociability and social presence of the robot, and increase the patient’s motivation, engagement and adherence. The video analysis shows that the gaze and social interaction with the robot were maintained throughout the CR programme, which is a valuable result showing that the patient did not lose interest in the robot throughout the long-term rehabilitation. Moreover, the patient (as well as the medical staff) acknowledged the robot as a social agent instead of just a tool, by verbally and non-verbally interacting with it. A detailed analysis of the perceived personalised aspects of the system showed that the patient positively reacted to the positive progress motivation given at the end of the session for having a lower number of problems in the session with “Let’s keep up the good work!”. In fact, the patient verbally thanked the robot in three of these cases, which did not happen towards the other non-personalised behaviours. The patient negatively reacted to the misidentiﬁcations in user recognition, which may further support the social agent perspective, however, he very positively responded to the corresponding UTAUT question as well as to the other personalisation aspects, which suggests that personalisation mitigates the negative user experience [29]. While the positive formulation of the Bond category of WAI also shows that the sociability of the robot was perceived highly positive throughout the CR programme, the negative formulation shows an increase in the social presence of the robot, based on the detailed analysis that indicated the fear of losing cooperation, and hence increased pressure to comply with the robot. In addition, even though the patient was mostly focused throughout the training stage, thereby limiting the gaze, the numbers indicate that the patient paid attention to the robot, thereby recognising its presence.

secao: IV. CASE STUDY > C. Long-term Perception of the Robot
trecho: Qualitative data was collected using the WAI questionnaire at the middle and end of the study, in order to analyse the long-term perception of the robot by the patient (Fig. 6). Results showed that the perception for Goal, Task and Bond was maintained highly positive throughout the CR programme, supporting our objectives with personalisation of the robot. Working Alliance Inventory (WAI) responses evaluated at the middle of the CR programme (18th session) and the ﬁnal (35th) session. In the case of negative formulation, the results decrease in Task and Goal category. These outcomes show that the negative perception of the robot decreases with time. The patient is less confused with the tasks (corrections) made by the robot during the rehabilitation, and the patient believes that the time spent with the robot is proﬁtable more over 4Conforming to normative behaviours to gain approval of another person. the duration of the CR programme. Regarding the Bond, the negative perception worsen slightly. Detailed analysis of the open questions showed that the patient felt that the robot would no longer cooperate with him during the sessions if he did not make the corrections requested by the robot (e.g., cervical posture and the high HR conﬁrmation). The UTAUT questionnaire [13] results support that the patient perceived the robot and the CR programme as highly positive, strongly agreeing with 88.5% of the questions and agreeing with the social presence aspects and the robot’s utility in therapy development, which is more positive than the perceptions of the non-personalised robot in [13]. Additionally, the personalisation aspects were all very positively perceived and enjoyed. The responses to the open questions further support the ﬁndings: “I would recommend using the robot as it is a great help during the CR programme”, “The robot interacts in a positive way with me, it helps me along with the medical staff, and it is also a good tool for them”.

As previously pointed out, personalisation helps improve user engagement and motivation throughout the sessions, which is critical for adherence to the CR programme. In addition, our previous work [13] indicated the need for increased sociability and social presence. Hence, we designed a personalised socially assistive robot. We recognise patients through a fully autonomous and online multi-modal user recognition system [25] that allows detecting and enrolling new users, without the need for any preliminary training. The user recognition combines face recognition with soft biometric (e.g., age, gender, and height) estimates obtained from NAOqi3 software of the robot, and the time of interaction of the patient to offer reliable user recognition in long-term HRI. In order to increase the sociability of the robot, we personalise the robot’s feedback by referring to the patient with his name periodically throughout the session. In addition, the progress of the patient (based on the number of alerts experienced) and the relative intensity of the sessions are tracked, which is used to motivate the patient for the current and upcoming sessions. (i) At the beginning of a session, the current session parameters are announced along with the relative intensity of the session and the previous session progress, such as “In the previous session, you experienced a problem with heart rate. I am sure it will be all ﬁne this 2https://www.softbankrobotics.com/emea/nao 3http://doc.aldebaran.com/2-5 time!”. The relative intensity is deﬁned (by the clinicians in FCI-IC) as higher if either the speed or inclination of the treadmill is higher than the previous session, and lower if both of these parameters are lower. (ii) At the end of the session, session progress is compared based on the relative intensity, e.g., “We had a lower number of problems in this session than the previous one, even though the session intensity was higher. Let’s keep up the good work, PATIENT NAME!” or “We had more problems... Next time will be better!”. In order to provide only positive feedback (as decided by the clinicians), we removed the comparison of the relative intensity if it was less intense.

In order to analyse the effects of the robot, quantitative and qualitative methods were used. The quantitative method is described by the physiological data acquired by the interface: heart rate (HR), Borg scale (BS) and systolic blood pressure (BP). In the case of the HR, the most important variables to the clinicians are the HR during the training stage, and the recovery HR corresponding to the difference between the HR at training and the HR acquired one minute after cooldown begins. Additionally, BS and BP were analysed to observe the exertion level and the effects of the exercise. For qualitative methods, we applied the Uniﬁed Theory of Acceptance and the Use of Technology (UTAUT) from our previous work [13], the Working Alliance Inventory (WAI) [14] and conducted a video analysis. The UTAUT questionnaire evaluates the perceived trust, safety, sociability, social presence, ease of use, utility and usefulness of the robot with positively formulated questions, in addition to open-ended questions for recommendations and additional comments. Additional custom questions were used to evaluate the perception and contentment of the personalisation aspects of the robot (i.e., recognition, using patient’s name, progress tracking, adherence motivation) corresponding to additional constructs, such as the perceived adaptivity, enjoyment and attitude towards the robot. The WAI questionnaire analyses three indicators (Task, Bond, and Goal) that allows evaluating the long-term interaction, with each item using negative (e.g., I feel uncomfortable with the help of the robot.) and positive (e.g., The robot perceives my objectives of the rehabilitation properly.) formulations that allows limiting the bias in the results. trecho: It is important to structure the social human-robot interaction such that the CR programme is not negatively affected, especially considering the medical context, the vulnerability of the patient, the potential of unanticipated events and the typical noise of a real-world environment [23]. As described in Sect.2.1.2, we collected feedback on perception and usability of the robot from all the subjects involved in the experiments, namely the healthy subjects, the physiotherapists, and the patients.

The platform used in the experiments presented in this paper is a R1 humanoid robot [9], developed by Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia (IIT). This platform is equipped with both standard color cameras and with depth cameras to better track the patient. It relies on wheels for navigating in the rooms, using a infrared laser (LIDAR) for obstacle avoidance. Finally, it is equipped with face expressions and speakers to afford interaction with the patients. In particular, in the developed “R1-TUG” functionality the robot engages the subject by verbally providing the instructions and indicating with its own arms at the same time the starting and ﬁnish lines of the test. The R1 robot then delivers the start signal with its synthesized voice. It uses its onboard AI-based vision system to acquire the movements of the limbs of the subject in the environment with the aim to extract online the parameters that are relevant to assess his/her balance and walking abilities. The subject can also ask R1 questions about the test, which the robot will be in turn able to answer leveraging on the natural-language processing system available in the cloud and accessible via the Google API. Finally, at the end of the test, the robot produces an extensive report for the clinician containing the assessment of the TUG parameters. The software used in this study, extends the architecture developed in [8] to evaluate lower limbs’ motions, follow the participants while continuously interacting with them, and verify that the test is completed successfully. An initial version of this software was presented in [10], where it was validated in a simulated environment. In this study, this software was deployed on the real robot and revised to deal noise coming from the robot’s sensors and to increase robustness while interacting with the real world and subjects.

Solutions leveraging humanoid embodied robots have been shown to engage patient engagement in rehab exercises [7, 8, 29]. Therefore, the goal of this work was also a preliminary evaluation of the effectiveness—in terms of usability, acceptability and perceived usefulness—of “R1-TUG” functionality to engage the end-users verbally and through face expressions, while providing correct feedback on the test. Concerning this aspect, the feedback received from healthy subjects indicates a usability perception (SUS = 68.33) which is just below the threshold of 70 points usually set for good product acceptability. This is also supported by the relatively high score in the Godspeed questionnaires received from healthy participants, in particular for the dimension of Likeability. Patients’ questionnaires show similar scores in the Goodspeed questionnaires, while they evaluated the usability better than the healthy volunteers (SUS = 81.33). Although this positive feedback should be interpreted cautiously, since patients did not directly experience the use of the robot, it represents a promising result for the future deployment of the TUG use case in a real clinical environment. ThetherapistsperceivedalowerusabilitylevelofR1(SUS = 47.5) compared to patients and healthy volunteers. This may be due to the current stage of development of the system, which is not yet ready to be used outside a laboratory environment, while therapists evaluated the solution already thinking of its application in their clinical practice. In conclusion, our results suggest the idea that using a Socially Assistive Robot to support the delivery of clinical tests within rehabilitation pathways could improve the ability of the physiotherapist to assess the subject’s movement performance, if compared to the standard clinical practice, while ensuring an adequate level of usability and acceptability form the participants.

secao: 2 Materials and Methods > 2.2 Humanoid Robot R1 Platform > 2.2.3 Speech Detection and Generation
trecho: As previously mentioned, R1 can interact verbally with the participants through a microphone and a speaker, both located in the robot head. When the subject wants to ask something to the robot about the exercise s-/he is going to perform, s-/he presses the button of a Wi-Fi controller he has in his own hand. This operation triggers the activation of the robot microphone, which records the audio clip and sends it to the googleSpeech module. This module acts as an interface between the robot and Google cloud services [21] which remotely process the stream returning a textual transcription of the user question. The provided string is then examined searching from speciﬁc keywords by the googleSpeechProcess module. If a match is found, a textual answer is then processed by googleSynthesis which generates an audio ﬁle with a synthetized voice starting from a text string. The system was developed to listen to subject’s questions only before starting the actual exercise and to answer only to a predeﬁned set of basic questions (e.g., which is the speed the participant should walk, if he needs to continue after reaching the ﬁnish line or if he can use a walking stick). In case the subject asks a question not in the preset, the system returns a “speech-error” event.

trecho: We used a set of questionnaires to collect the perception of the robot TUG functionalities from the potential end-users (subjects- healthy volunteers and patients- and physiotherapists) point of view in terms of usability, acceptability, and perceived usefulness. In particular, the following surveys were used: • System Usability Scale (SUS) [11]. It is frequently used scale to measure acceptability and usability of technologicalsolutionswithwell-assessedpsychometricproperties [12]. It includes 10 statements and the compilers have useful for evaluating patients balance and mobility I think my hospital would be available to adopt a solution like this to automatize rehabilitation tests like TUG to declare their level of agreement with each item on a 1–5 scale (between “strongly disagree” 1 and “strongly agree” 5). The overall SUS score ranges from 0 to 100; • Godspeed Questionnaire Series (GQS) [13]. It has been speciﬁcally developed to evaluate the perception of social interaction with robots- especially humanoids- and to benchmark solutions in the ﬁeld of Human–Robot Interaction [14, 15]. It allows to analyse robotic solutions on different aspects. In particular, for our study we selected the following dimensions: antropomorphism, animacy, likeability and perceived intelligence. Details on pychometric properties can be found in [16]; • Ad hoc questionnaire for physiotherapists Differently from a standard questionnaire, the ad hoc option allowed us to investigate speciﬁc aspects of the proposed solution, to collect desiderata from the end-users and, therefore, useful insights for the future development of the robot. In particular, this questionnaire investigates the perceived usefulness and appropriateness of the R1-TUG solution from the physiotherapists point of view. Similarly to the SUS scale, the questionnaire requires the compilers to declare their level of agreement with each of the 12 items on a 1–5 scale (between “strongly disagree” 1 and “strongly agree” 5). The items of the questionnaire are reported in Table 1.

Fifteen patients evaluated the R1 TUG functionality after having watched a video of the tests performed by healthy volunteers. They provided their feedback through the SUS scale, the GSQ and free text comments and suggestions- results in Table 4. System Usability Scale (SUS) The mean value of the SUS scores received from the 15 patients was 81.33 (SD = 18.54). The SUS items obtaining on average the worst results are the number 1 “I think that I would like to use this system frequently” and the number 10 “I think I would need to learn a lot of things before I could get going with this system”. On the other hand, the two items achieving the best results are the number 8 “I found the system very cumbersome to use” and number 2 “I found the system unnecessarily complex”. The scores of the SUS questionnaire indicate a good acceptability level from the patients’ point of view. This is an encouraging result, although it must be interpreted cautiously since the patients did not have the possibility of testing the system in ﬁrst person. Godspeed Questionnaire Series (GSQ) The R1 robot achieved good results in terms of Perceived Intelligence and Likeability. These positives results, which are in line with the ones of healthy volunteers, are encouraging in terms of the acceptability of the robot from patients.

Although the number of patients in each condition is limited, this work serves as a pilot study to provide a first view on the ability of the system to provide reliable information and to analyze the interaction between the users and the system. During the experiment, we observed that patients in the RoC scenario seem to be more compliant with the requests that the robot made along the sessions compared to patients in the NRoC condition. Results show an average response time of 12 seconds in RoC, while for NRoC this was 28 seconds. This is a positive aspect that shows promise for an embodied agent within the sessions. It was also possible to observe that the system is able to assess some of the aforementioned risk factors and make effective interventions to reduce them. On the other hand, there was no observable pattern in the heart rate recovery between two scenarios. However, in the long-term experiments this metric might be significant in order to compare how well patients improve their physical condition on each scenario. According to the third metric described above, the motivation results from all patients was 10 for both questions, indicating that all of them had felt very well during the sessions and are motivated to come back. Since all the results are the same, it is not possible to carry out any comparison between the two scenarios.

One of the most critical issues in CR is the lack of adherence of patients to the rehabilitation process. Warning: when any of the aforementioned risk factors is perceived, the robot enters the warning state. The most important risk factor to control is the unexpected increase in the heart rate. Once an increment of this parameter is perceived, the robot asks the patient whether everything is fine or medical staff should be called. If the patient reports that everything is going well, the therapy continues normally. However, if the response is negative or a response is lacking, the robot changes to the Emergency state. Another risk factor that is controlled in this state is dizziness and the possibility of falling. To avoid this issue, the robot monitors the patient’s posture with a camera and asks the patient to correct its posture. Emergency: this state is triggered when the existence of a risk factor is confirmed and can be set in three different scenarios: (1) when the warning state changes to the emergency state; (2) when the robot detects an excessive increase in heart rate, and (3) when the alarm is triggered by the patient through the GUI (pain, dizziness or fatigue). The robot alerts the medical staff while indicating the type of the emergency. Four patients were divided into two groups (No robot condition (NRoC) and Robot Condition (RoC)) in order to compare the first 4 sessions of each patient in a preliminary study. Three metrics were considered for the evaluation of the therapy: response time, heart rate recovery and motivation. The response time measures how compliant the patient is to a request for reporting the BS value, which corresponds to the time between the system request of BS and input time from the patient in seconds. Heart rate recovery measures the evolution of the heart rate (BPM) during the first minute of the cool-down phase. The motivation of the patient is acquired at the end of the session, through a Likert scale (0 to 10, 0 not motivated at all and 10 very motivated) with "How was the session today?" and "How motivated do you feel to come back?".

Although the number of patients in each condition is limited, this work serves as a pilot study to provide a first view on the ability of the system to provide reliable information and to analyze the interaction between the users and the system. During the experiment, we observed that patients in the RoC scenario seem to be more compliant with the requests that the robot made along the sessions compared to patients in the NRoC condition. Results show an average response time of 12 seconds in RoC, while for NRoC this was 28 seconds. This is a positive aspect that shows promise for an embodied agent within the sessions. It was also possible to observe that the system is able to assess some of the aforementioned risk factors and make effective interventions to reduce them. On the other hand, there was no observable pattern in the heart rate recovery between two scenarios. However, in the long-term experiments this metric might be significant in order to compare how well patients improve their physical condition on each scenario. According to the third metric described above, the motivation results from all patients was 10 for both questions, indicating that all of them had felt very well during the sessions and are motivated to come back. Since all the results are the same, it is not possible to carry out any comparison between the two scenarios.

[12] highlighted that robots for stroke rehabilitation should include two guiding principles: (1) intensity of task-specific training and (2) engagement and self-management of goal-directed actions. In the robotbased system that we developed, we followed these guidelines with the addition of the guidelines that we will elaborate on here. One of the most notable requirements of SAR for rehabilitation, that was stressed in the focus groups discussion, is the need for personalization of the system. Feingold-Polak et al. [15], Eizicovits et al. [22], Kashi & Levy-Tzedek [23], and Clabaugh and Matarić [24] also highlighted the importance of personalizing the design of HRI and tailoring it to the specific task. This is of high significance in vulnerable populations such as neurological impaired patients, where robots can assist in maintaining a training regime and establishment of long-term trust between the user and the robot is essential [25]. Stroke patients often depend on reliable and effective relationships with their therapists. They are often older and multi-morbid and suffer from psychological distress because of their disability [25]. Thus, in order for the robotic device to be effective for therapy and accepted by both the patient and the clinician, it has to be flexible and adjustable, taking into account the complexity of the specific impairment. For the experience of the user to be positive, and to achieve engagement in the task, it is important to personalize the interaction according to the age, the needs of the user and the characteristics of the task.

Robots that are designed for sensorimotor rehabilitation should be adaptable so they can be adjusted to each patient individually. For a system to be applicable to a wide variety of patients and different levels of impairments, and in order for it to engage patients in the long-term, there should be a variety of tasks, at different levels, applicable for both low-functioning and highfunctioning patients. Users should be able to progress in the task according to their ability and performance. The instructions given to the user should be simple, gradually increasing in difficulty, and spoken slowly and clearly. The response time of the robot, however, should be fast [15]. Patients should have the ability to rest when needed, but not for too long. When the patient is fatigued and cannot complete the task without using undesired compensatory movements, the session should end. The robot provided instruction, feedback, and motivation. The instruction was provided at the beginning of each session, the beginning of each bout, and when users made errors. At the beginning of each session, the robot described the rules and goals of the wire puzzle task. At the beginning of each bout, the robot told the user which wand to use, and pointed to the wand with its right hand. Whenever the user made an error, such as using the wrong wand or failing to moving the wand in the right direction, the robot reiterated the task instructions. Feedback was provided at the end of each bout. The robot provided knowledge of performance in the form of movement time and the number of errors. For example, it said: “You took ﬁve seconds, and touched the wire four times.” In addition to verbalizing performance results, the robot nodded its head with an amplitude proportional to the user’s performance. Motivation was provided in the form of verbalized encouraging statements (e.g., “good job”, “congratulations”). Further, the robot made congratulatory gestures (e.g., moving its arms up and down in a cheering motion) in response to improved performance. In addition to the measures described in the previous section (puzzle and IMU data), we also collected fatigue and psychometric data. We collected self–reported fatigue measures at the start and end of each 15–minute session, and survey data regarding the quality and quantity of the robot gestures and verbalizations at the end of each day. We also obtained data regarding the perceived usefulness of the task with a survey based on the valid and reliable Intrinsic Motivation Index scale [23].

secao: VI. DISCUSSION > C. Automated Robot–Guided Intervention
trecho: We reiterate here that the intervention was administered completely autonomously by the SAR robot, based on observations of the user state obtained from the various sensor modalities. This study thus shows that our SAR system can be used to affect desirable behavior changes in some individuals post–stroke, but studies with larger sample sizes are needed to determine if the results are statistically signiﬁcant. To properly adapt the system, data from this study can be used to characterize a range of UE FMA scores for which the task, as designed, is appropriate. While this will be beneﬁcial to the population, it will also allow us to gain more insight into the human–robot interaction, as the task will be more directly matched to the participants’ challenge level. Evidence has shown that maintaining an appropriate challenge level in human–human interactions has a number of beneﬁts, both physical and psychological [26]. If we can more adequately maintain challenge level, we can take advantage of these beneﬁts to strengthen SAR-guided interaction.

secao: III. SAR SYSTEM FOR MOTOR TASK PRACTICE > A. Physical Setup
trecho: The physical setup for our SAR system consisted of a humanoid robot torso, an instrumented wire puzzle, and wearable sensors. The robot used in our experiments is the humanoid Bandit, developed at the USC Interaction Laboratory in conjunction with BlueSky Robotics (Figure 1). We have used Bandit in a variety of SAR interactions in the past [17] [18] [6]. In this study, Bandit was used to guide participants during the performance of a wire puzzle game (Figure 2). Participants were seated at a desk facing Bandit and the puzzle and had a selection of wands; the goal was to guide the ring at the end of each wand along the wire puzzle without contacting the wire (Figure 3). Bandit used two different “coaching styles:” in one, Bandit instructed the participants which wand to use, while in the other, they chose the wand themselves. Task difﬁculty was controlled by appropriately selecting wands with smaller or larger diameters, and puzzles with lower or higher complexity (wire curvature). A Phidget InterfaceKit was used to electrically instrument the puzzles; this allowed us to collect error (total number of contacts between the ring and puzzle) and movement time data. Participant arm motion was monitored using an inertial measurement unit (IMU) also developed in our laboratory [22]. The IMU captured 3–axis each of accelerometer, rate gyroscope, and magnetometer data. The complete experimental setup is shown in Figure 2. secao: II. BACKGROUND > B. Socially Assistive Robotics
trecho: The ﬁeld of socially assistive robotics (SAR) is a newer development and is deﬁned as the provision of assistance through social (not physical) interactions with robots [1]. A SAR robot uses non–contact verbal and non–verbal feedback, coaching, and encouragement to guide a user during the performance of a task. SAR systems can demonstrate task goals, monitor the user, and provide extrinsic performance feedback. The lack of physical contact means there are a minimum of safety concerns. Further advantages include lower costs and increased accessibility relative to contact– based robot systems. A SAR interaction can take place in a multitude of environments, including the laboratory, the clinic, and the user’s home. Our past work has shown the efﬁcacy of SAR in a variety of domains, including elder care [17] [18], Autism Spectrum Disorders [19], stroke assessment [20] [21], and stroke rehabilitation [7]. A key advantage of non–contact SAR over contact–based robotics in the stroke population is that individuals can use the more affected limb in the types of meaningful, unconstrained, functional tasks encountered in daily life. This approach also has the ability to provide personalized therapeutic interactions that can complement the therapist. We view SAR as complementary to contact–based rehabilitation systems, with its usefulness being especially targeted toward post–acute stages of stroke rehabilitation, which have been shown to potentially continue life-long. In the following, we describe the implementation of our SAR system for intense, task–speciﬁc training for post–stroke rehabilitation and present preliminary results. trecho: We reiterate here that the intervention was administered completely autonomously by the SAR robot, based on observations of the user state obtained from the various sensor modalities. This study thus shows that our SAR system can be used to affect desirable behavior changes in some individuals post–stroke, but studies with larger sample sizes are needed to determine if the results are statistically signiﬁcant. To properly adapt the system, data from this study can be used to characterize a range of UE FMA scores for which the task, as designed, is appropriate. While this will be beneﬁcial to the population, it will also allow us to gain more insight into the human–robot interaction, as the task will be more directly matched to the participants’ challenge level. Evidence has shown that maintaining an appropriate challenge level in human–human interactions has a number of beneﬁts, both physical and psychological [26]. If we can more adequately maintain challenge level, we can take advantage of these beneﬁts to strengthen SAR-guided interaction.

The robot provided instruction, feedback, and motivation. The instruction was provided at the beginning of each session, the beginning of each bout, and when users made errors. At the beginning of each session, the robot described the rules and goals of the wire puzzle task. At the beginning of each bout, the robot told the user which wand to use, and pointed to the wand with its right hand. Whenever the user made an error, such as using the wrong wand or failing to moving the wand in the right direction, the robot reiterated the task instructions. Feedback was provided at the end of each bout. The robot provided knowledge of performance in the form of movement time and the number of errors. For example, it said: “You took ﬁve seconds, and touched the wire four times.” In addition to verbalizing performance results, the robot nodded its head with an amplitude proportional to the user’s performance. Motivation was provided in the form of verbalized encouraging statements (e.g., “good job”, “congratulations”). Further, the robot made congratulatory gestures (e.g., moving its arms up and down in a cheering motion) in response to improved performance. In addition to the measures described in the previous section (puzzle and IMU data), we also collected fatigue and psychometric data. We collected self–reported fatigue measures at the start and end of each 15–minute session, and survey data regarding the quality and quantity of the robot gestures and verbalizations at the end of each day.
